name: K Visa (STEM professional, no employer sponsor required)

requirements.blocker_text: Requires academic or professional qualifications in a science, technology, engineering, or mathematics field prioritised by China's government -- this is the K visa's defining feature versus the Z visa: no pre-arranged employer sponsor is required at the application stage.
requirements.fix_path: Document qualifications in a qualifying STEM field.

requirements.blocker_text: Requires demonstrated financial self-sufficiency for the intended stay, since there is no employer sponsor providing income verification at the application stage.
requirements.fix_path: Document sufficient personal funds or alternative income sources.

evidence_required.document: Academic credentials or professional qualifications in a qualifying STEM field

outcome.duration_length: not conclusively established in this research pass; treated as a multi-entry, multi-year status pending confirmation

sources.title: Immigration World -- China Immigration Guide 2026, describing the K Visa introduced in 2024 for STEM professionals entering without a pre-arranged employer sponsor

notes: HONEST SOURCING GAP, one of the thinnest in this build: the K visa is a genuinely new policy (introduced 2024) and only a single tier-3 source was found describing it in this research pass -- no other independent source, and no nia.gov.cn or Ministry of Foreign Affairs page, was successfully located or fetched to corroborate its specific mechanics. Several outcome fields (duration_length, family_can_join, family_can_work) are left honestly unconfirmed rather than guessed, consistent with this project's sourcing discipline -- this is a genuine open question for a follow-up session rather than an asserted fact. leads_to_pr and leads_to_citizenship are conservatively set to false rather than assumed, since no source confirmed a direct pathway; switchable_to points to cn_z_visa_work_permit as the more likely practical route to settlement once a K-visa holder secures employer sponsorship, mirroring how China's other STEM/talent-adjacent policies generally funnel back into the standard employer-sponsored system rather than offering an independent settlement ladder. If confirmed accurate on further research, this would be a genuinely notable structural finding: a mainland Chinese work-entry route requiring no employer sponsor at all is a first in this dataset's East Asian country set (Korea's closest analogue, F-2-7, still requires prior E-/D-visa status first) -- but this claim rests on a single source and should be treated with appropriate caution until independently verified.
